entries.7a9965b9b189a2249a6226b902fbb4e619b2ceb3: <div sID="gen17946" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="34" osisID="Jer.34" sID="Jer.34"/> <div eID="gen17946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17947" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17948" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have two messages which God sent by Jeremiah. I. One to foretel the fate of Zedekiah king of Judah, that he should fall into the hands of the king of Babylon, that he should live a captive, but should at last die in peace in his captivity, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. Another to read the doom both of prince and people for their treacherous dealings with God, in bringing back into bondage their servants whom they had released according to the law, and so playing fast and loose with God. They had walked at all adventures with God (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.11">ver. 8-11</reference>), and therefore God would walk at all adventures with them, in bringing the Chaldean army upon them again when they began to hope that they had got clear of them, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.12-Jer.34.22">ver. 12-22</reference>.
entries.0e1cd7cffaf80a8a304e81880fdc99853bdd035a: <div eID="gen17948" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17947" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Captivity of Zedekiah Foretold; The Babylonish Captivity Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen17949" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word which came unto Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and all his army, and all the kingdoms of the earth of his dominion, and all the people, fought against Jerusalem, and against all the cities thereof, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of Israel; Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah, and tell him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire: <hi type="super">3</hi> And thou shalt not escape out of his hand, but shalt surely be taken, and delivered into his hand; and thine eyes shall behold the eyes of the king of Babylon, and he shall speak with thee mouth to mouth, and thou shalt go to Babylon. <hi type="super">4</hi> Yet hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O Zedekiah king of Judah; Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of thee, Thou shalt not die by the sword: <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">But</hi> thou shalt die in peace: and with the burnings of thy fathers, the former kings which were before thee, so shall they burn <hi type="italic">odours</hi> for thee; and they will lament thee, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Ah lord! for I have pronounced the word, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> Then Jeremiah the prophet spake all these words unto Zedekiah king of Judah in Jerusalem, <hi type="super">7</hi> When the king of Babylon's army fought against Jerusalem, and against all the cities of Judah that were left, against Lachish, and against Azekah: for these defenced cities remained of the cities of Judah. <div eID="gen17949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17950" type="x-p"/> This prophecy concerning Zedekiah was delivered to Jeremiah, and by him to the parties concerned, before he was shut up in the prison, for we find this prediction here made the ground of his commitment, as appears by the recital of some passages out of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.4">ch. xxxii. 4</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen17950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17951" type="x-p"/> I. The time when this message was sent to Zedekiah; it was <hi type="italic">when the king of Babylon,</hi> with all his forces, some out of <hi type="italic">all the kingdoms of the earth</hi> that were within his jurisdiction, <hi type="italic">fought against Jerusalem and the cities thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.1">v. 1</reference>), designing to destroy them, having often plundered them. The cities that now remained, and yet held out, are named (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Lachish and Azekah.</hi> This intimates that things were now brought to the last extremity, and yet Zedekiah obstinately stood it out, his heart being hardened to his destruction. <div eID="gen17951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17952" type="x-p"/> II. The message itself that was sent to him. 1. Here is a threatening of wrath. He is told that again which he had been often told before, that the city shall be taken by the Chaldeans <hi type="italic">and burnt with fire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.2">v. 2</reference>), that he shall himself fall into the enemy's hands, shall be made a prisoner, shall be brought before that furious prince Nebuchadnezzar, and be carried away captive into Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.3">v. 3</reference>); yet Ezekiel prophesied that he <hi type="italic">should not see Babylon;</hi> nor did he, for his eyes were put out, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Ezek. xii. 13</reference>. This Zedekiah brought upon himself from God by his other sins and from Nebuchadnezzar by breaking his faith with him. 2. Here is a mixture of mercy. He shall die a captive, but he <hi type="italic">shall not die by the sword</hi> he shall die a natural death (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.4">v. 4</reference>); he shall end his days with some comfort, <hi type="italic">shall die in peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">v. 5</reference>. He never had been one of the worst of the kings, but we are willing to hope that what evil he had <hi type="italic">done in the sight of the Lord</hi> he repented of in his captivity, as Manasseh had done, and it was forgiven to him; and, God being reconciled to him, he might truly be said to <hi type="italic">die in peace,</hi> Note, A man may die in a prison and yet <hi type="italic">die in peace.</hi> Nay, he shall end his days with some reputation, more than one would expect, all things considered. He shall be buried <hi type="italic">with the burnings of his fathers,</hi> that is, with the respect usually shown to their kings, especially those that had done good in Israel. It seems, in his captivity he had conducted himself so well towards his own people that they were willing to do him this honour, and towards Nebuchadnezzar that he suffered it to be done. If Zedekiah had continued in his prosperity, perhaps he would have grown worse and would have <hi type="italic">departed</hi> at last <hi type="italic">without being desired;</hi> but his afflictions wrought such a change in him that his death was looked upon as a great loss. It is better to live and die penitent in a prison than to live and die impenitent in a palace. <hi type="italic">They will lament thee, saying, Ah lord!</hi> an honour which his brother Jehoiakim had not, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.18">ch. xxii. 18</reference>. The Jews say that they lamented thus over him, <hi type="italic">Alas! Zedekiah is dead, who drank the dregs of all the ages that went before him,</hi> that is, who suffered for the sins of his ancestors, the measure of iniquity being filled up in his days. They shall thus lament him, <hi type="italic">saith the Lord, for I have pronounced the word;</hi> and what God hath spoken shall without fail be made good. <div eID="gen17952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17953" type="x-p"/> III. Jeremiah's faithfulness in delivering this message. Though he knew it would be ungrateful to the king, and might prove, as indeed it did, dangerous to himself (for he was imprisoned for it), yet he <hi type="italic">spoke all these words to Zedekiah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.6">v. 6</reference>. It is a mercy to great men to have those about them that will deal faithfully with them, and tell them the evil consequences of their evil courses, that they may reform and live.
entries.f499c050070074fcaa2ddfb9d43526d2ced2a488: <div eID="gen17953" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Transient Reformation; The Servants Re-enslaved. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen17954" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">This is</hi> the word that came unto Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , after that the king Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people which <hi type="italic">were</hi> at Jerusalem, to proclaim liberty unto them; <hi type="super">9</hi> That every man should let his manservant, and every man his maidservant, <hi type="italic">being</hi> a Hebrew or a Hebrewess, go free; that none should serve himself of them, <hi type="italic">to wit,</hi> of a Jew his brother. <hi type="super">10</hi> Now when all the princes, and all the people, which had entered into the covenant, heard that every one should let his manservant, and every one his maidservant, go free, that none should serve themselves of them any more, then they obeyed, and let <hi type="italic">them</hi> go. <hi type="super">11</hi> But afterward they turned, and caused the servants and the handmaids, whom they had let go free, to return, and brought them into subjection for servants and for handmaids. <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came to Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">13</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of Israel; I made a covenant with your fathers in the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondmen, saying, <hi type="super">14</hi> At the end of seven years let ye go every man his brother an Hebrew, which hath been sold unto thee; and when he hath served thee six years, thou shalt let him go free from thee: but your fathers hearkened not unto me, neither inclined their ear. <hi type="super">15</hi> And ye were now turned, and had done right in my sight, in proclaiming liberty every man to his neighbour; and ye had made a covenant before me in the house which is called by my name: <hi type="super">16</hi> But ye turned and polluted my name, and caused every man his servant, and every man his handmaid, whom ye had set at liberty at their pleasure, to return, and brought them into subjection, to be unto you for servants and for handmaids. <hi type="super">17</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Ye have not hearkened unto me, in proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother, and every man to his neighbour: behold, I proclaim a liberty for you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine; and I will make you to be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth. <hi type="super">18</hi> And I will give the men that have transgressed my covenant, which have not performed the words of the covenant which they had made before me, when they cut the calf in twain, and passed between the parts thereof, <hi type="super">19</hi> The princes of Judah, and the princes of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, and the priests, and all the people of the land, which passed between the parts of the calf; <hi type="super">20</hi> I will even give them into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of them that seek their life: and their dead bodies shall be for meat unto the fowls of the heaven, and to the beasts of the earth. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Zedekiah king of Judah and his princes will I give into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of them that seek their life, and into the hand of the king of Babylon's army, which are gone up from you. <hi type="super">22</hi> Behold, I will command, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and cause them to return to this city; and they shall fight against it, and take it, and burn it with fire: and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without an inhabitant. <div eID="gen17954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17955" type="x-p"/> We have here another prophecy upon a particular occasion, the history of which we must take notice of, as necessary to give light to the prophecy. <div eID="gen17955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17956" type="x-p"/> I. When Jerusalem was closely besieged by the Chaldean army the princes and people agreed upon a reformation in one instance, and that was concerning their servants. <div eID="gen17956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17957" type="x-p"/> 1. The law of God was very express, that those of their own nation should not be held in servitude above seven years, but, after they had served one apprenticeship, they should be discharged and have their liberty; yea, though they had sold themselves into servitude for the payment of their debts, or though they were <hi type="italic">sold by the judges</hi> for the punishment of their crimes. This difference was put between their brethren and strangers, that those of other nations taken in war, or bought with money, might be held in perpetual slavery, they and theirs; but their brethren must serve but for seven years at the longest. This God calls the covenant that he had made with them when he <hi type="italic">brought them out of the land of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.13-Jer.34.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. This was the first of the judicial laws which God gave them (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.2">Exod. xxi. 2</reference>), and there was good reason for this law. (1.) God had put honour upon that nation, and he would have them thus to preserve the honour of it themselves and to put a difference between it and other nations. (2.) God had brought them out of slavery in Egypt, and he would have them thus to express their grateful sense of that favour, by letting those go to whom their houses were <hi type="italic">houses of bondage,</hi> as Egypt had been to their forefathers. That deliverance is therefore mentioned here (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.13">v. 13</reference>) as the ground of that law. Note, God's compassions towards us should engage our compassions towards our brethren; we must release as we are released, forgive as we are forgiven, and relieve as we are relieved. And this is called <hi type="italic">a covenant;</hi> for our performance of the duty required is the condition of the continuance of the favours God has bestowed. <div eID="gen17957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17958" type="x-p"/> 2. This law they and their fathers had broken. Their worldly profit swayed more with them than God's command or covenant. When their servants had lived seven years with them they understood their business, and how to apply themselves to it, better than they did when they first came to them, and therefore they would then by no means part with them, though God himself by his law had made them free: <hi type="italic">Your fathers hearkened not to me</hi> in this matter (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.14">v. 14</reference>), so that from the days of their fathers they had been in this trespass; and they thought they might do it because their fathers did it, and their servants had by disuse lost the benefit of the provision God made for them; whereas against an express law, especially against an express law of God, no custom, usage, nor prescription, is to be admitted in plea. For this sin of theirs, and their fathers, God now brought them into servitude, and justly. <div eID="gen17958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17959" type="x-p"/> 3. When they were besieged, and closely shut in, by the army of the Chaldeans, they, being told of their fault in this matter, immediately reformed, and let go all their servants that were entitled to their freedom by the law of God, as Pharaoh, who, when the plague was upon him, consented to <hi type="italic">let the people go,</hi> and bound themselves in a covenant to do so. (1.) The prophets faithfully admonished them concerning their sin. From them they heard that they should let their Hebrew servants <hi type="italic">go free,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.10">v. 10</reference>. They might have read it themselves in the book of the law, but did not, or did not heed it, therefore the prophets told them what the law was. See what need there is of the preaching of the word; people must hear the word preached because they will not make the use they ought to make of the word written. (2.) All orders and degrees of men concurred in this reformation. The <hi type="italic">king,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">princes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all the people,</hi> agreed to <hi type="italic">let go their servants,</hi> whatever loss or damage they might sustain by so doing. When the king and princes led in this good work the people could not for shame but follow. The example and influence of great men would go very far towards extirpating the most inveterate corruptions. (3.) They bound themselves by a solemn oath and covenant that they would do this, whereby they engaged themselves to God and one another. Note, What God has bound us to by his precept, it is good for us to bind ourselves to by our promise. This covenant was very solemn: it was made in a sacred place, <hi type="italic">made before me, in the house which is called by my name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.15">v. 15</reference>), in the special presence of God, the tokens of which, in the temple, ought to strike an awe upon them and make them very sincere in their appeals to him. It was ratified by a significant sign; they <hi type="italic">cut a calf in two, and passed between the parts thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.18-Jer.34.19">v. 18, 19</reference>) with this dreadful imprecation, "Let us be in like manner cut asunder if we do not perform what we now promise." This calf was probably offered up in sacrifice to God, who was thereby made a party to the covenant. When God covenanted with Abraham, for the ratification of it, a <hi type="italic">smoking furnace</hi> and a <hi type="italic">burning lamp passed between the pieces</hi> of the sacrifice, in allusion to this federal rite, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Gen. xv. 17</reference>. Note, In order that we may effectually oblige ourselves to our duty, it is good to alarm ourselves with the apprehensions of the terror of the wrath and curse to which we expose ourselves if we live in the contempt of it, that wrath which will <hi type="italic">cut sinners asunder</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.51">Matt. xxiv. 51</reference>), and sensible signs may be of use to make the impressions of it deep and durable, as here. (4.) They conformed themselves herein to the command of God and their covenant with him; they did <hi type="italic">let their servants go,</hi> though at this time, when the city was besieged, they could very ill spare them. Thus they did <hi type="italic">right in God's sight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.15">v. 15</reference>. Though it was their trouble that drove them to it, yet he was well pleased with it; and if they had persevered in this act of <hi type="italic">mercy to the poor,</hi> to their poor servants, it might have been a lengthening of their tranquillity, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Dan. iv. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen17959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17960" type="x-p"/> II. When there was some hope that the siege was raised and the danger over they repented of their repentance, undid the good they had done, and forced the servants they had released into their respective services again. 1. The <hi type="italic">king of Babylon's army</hi> had now <hi type="italic">gone up from them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.21">v. 21</reference>. Pharaoh was bringing an army of Egyptians to oppose the progress of the king of Babylon's victories, upon the tidings of which the Chaldeans raised the siege for a time, as we find, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">ch. xxxvii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">They departed from Jerusalem.</hi> See how ready God was to put a stop to his judgments, upon the first instance of reformation, so slow is he to anger and so swift to show mercy. As soon as ever they let their servants go free God let them go free. 2. When they began to think themselves safe from the besiegers they made their servants come back into subjection to them, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.11">v. 11</reference>, and again <reference osisRef="Jer.34.16">v. 16</reference>. This was a great abuse to their servants, to whom servitude would be more irksome, after they had had some taste of the pleasures of liberty. It was a great shame to themselves that they could not keep in a good mind when they were in it. But it was especially an affront to God; in doing this they <hi type="italic">polluted his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.16">v. 16</reference>. It was a contempt of the command he had given them, as if that were of no force at all, but they might either keep it or break it as they thought fit. It was a contempt of the covenant they had made with him, and of that wrath which they had imprecated upon themselves in case they should break that covenant. It was jesting with God almighty, as if he could be imposed upon by fallacious promises, which, when they had gained their point, they would look upon themselves no longer obliged by. it was <hi type="italic">lying to God with their mouths</hi> and <hi type="italic">flattering him with their tongues.</hi> It was likewise a contempt of the judgments of God and setting them at defiance; as if, when once the course of them was stopped a little and interrupted, they would never proceed again and the judgment would never be revived; whereas reprieves are so far from being pardons that if they be abused thus, and sinners take encouragement from them to return to sin, they are but preparatives for heavier strokes of divine vengeance. <div eID="gen17960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17961" type="x-p"/> III. For this treacherous dealing with God they are here severely threatened. <hi type="italic">Be not deceived; God is not mocked.</hi> Those that think to put a cheat upon God by a dissembled repentance, a fallacious covenant, and a partial temporary reformation, will prove in the end to have put the greatest cheat upon their own souls; for <hi type="italic">the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.</hi> It is here threatened, with an observable air of displeasure against them, 1. That, since they had not given liberty to their servants to go where they pleased, God would give all his judgments liberty to take their course against them without control (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have not proclaimed liberty to your servants.</hi> Though they had done it (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.10">v. 10</reference>), yet they might truly be said not to have done it, because they did not stand to it, but undid it again; and <hi type="italic">factum non dicitur quod non perseverat—that is not said to be done which does not last.</hi> The righteousness that is forsaken and turned away from shall be forgotten, and <hi type="italic">not mentioned</hi> any more than if it had never been, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.24">Ezek. xviii. 24</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Therefore I will proclaim a liberty for you;</hi> I will discharge you from my service, and put you out of my protection, which those forfeit that withdraw from their allegiance. You shall have liberty to choose which of these judgments you will be cut off by, <hi type="italic">sword, famine, or pestilence;</hi>" such a liberty as was offered to David, which put him into a <hi type="italic">great strait,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.14">2 Sam. xxiv. 14</reference>. Note, Those that will not be in subjection to the law of God put themselves into subjection to the wrath and curse of God. But this shows what liberty to <hi type="italic">sin</hi> really—it is but a liberty to the sorest judgments. 2. That, since they had brought their servants back into confinement in their houses, God would <hi type="italic">make them to be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth,</hi> where they should live in servitude, and, being strangers, could not expect the privileges of free-born subjects. 3. That, since they had broken the covenant which they ratified by a solemn imprecation, God would bring on them the evil which they imprecated upon themselves in case they should break it. Out of their own mouth will he judge them, and so shall their doom be; the penalty of their bond shall be recovered, because they have not performed the condition; for so some read <reference osisRef="Jer.34.18">v. 18</reference>, "<hi type="italic">I will make the men which have transgressed my covenant as the calf which they cut in twain;</hi> I will divide them asunder as they divided it asunder." 4. That, since they would not let go their servants out of the hands, God would deliver them into the hands of those that hated them, even <hi type="italic">the princes</hi> and nobles both <hi type="italic">of Judah and Jerusalem</hi> (of the country and of the city), <hi type="italic">the eunuchs</hi> (chamberlains, or great officers of the court), <hi type="italic">the priests, and all the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.19">v. 19</reference>. They had all dealt treacherously with God, and therefore shall all be involved in the common ruin without exception. They shall all be <hi type="italic">given unto the hand of their enemies, that seek,</hi> not their wealth only, or their service, but <hi type="italic">their life,</hi> and they shall have what they seek; but neither shall that content them: when they have their lives they shall leave <hi type="italic">their dead bodies</hi> unburied, a loathsome spectacle to all mankind and an easy prey to <hi type="italic">the fowls and beasts,</hi> a lasting mark of ignominy being hereby fastened on them, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.20">v. 20</reference>. 5. That, since they had emboldened themselves in returning to their sin, contrary to their covenant, by the retreat of the Chaldean army from them, God would therefore bring it upon them again: "They have now <hi type="italic">gone up from you,</hi> and your fright is over for the present, but I <hi type="italic">will command them</hi> to face about as they were; they shall <hi type="italic">return to this city, and take it and burn it,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.34.22">v. 22</reference>. Note, (1.) As confidence in God is a hopeful presage of approaching deliverance, so security in sin is a sad omen of approaching destruction. (2.) When judgments are removed from a people before they have done their work, leave them, but leave them unhumbled and unreformed, it is <hi type="italic">cum animo revertendi</hi>—<hi type="italic">with a design to return;</hi> they do but retreat to come on again with so much the greater force; for when God judges he will overcome. (3.) It is just with God to disappoint those expectations of mercy which his providence had given cause for when we disappoint those expectations of duty which our professions, pretensions, and fair promises, had given cause for. If we repent of the good we had purposed, God will repent of the good he had purposed. <hi type="italic">With the froward thou will show thyself froward.</hi>  <chapter eID="Jer.34"/> <div eID="gen17961" type="x-p"/>

entries.8880b997c3f302aa14a2cb6019026aa0dd58c2b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10354"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 34</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.22">Jr 34:1-22</reference>. Captivity of Zedekiah and the People Foretold for Their Disobedience and Perfidy.</title> <div sID="gen18476" type="x-p"/> The prophecy (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7">Jr 34:1-7</reference>) as to Zedekiah is an amplification of that in <reference osisRef="Jer.32.1-Jer.32.5">Jr 32:1-5</reference>, in consequence of which Jeremiah was then shut up in the court of the prison. The prophecy (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.22">Jr 34:8-22</reference>) refers to the Jews, who, afraid of the capture of the city, had, in obedience to the law, granted freedom to their servants at the end of seven years, but on the intermission of the siege forced them back into bondage.<div eID="gen18476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10354"/><hi type="bold">1. Jerusalem and ... all the cities thereof--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Jer.19.15">Jr 19:15</reference>). It was amazing blindness in the king, that, in such a desperate position, he should reject admonition. <div eID="gen18477" type="x-p"/>

entries.de8be837184e19d288f01bbbb3657623df96e208: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10358"/><div sID="gen18482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10358"/><hi type="bold">7. these ... retained--</hi>alone (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.5">2Ch 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen18482" type="x-p"/>
entries.f14de2a7d9b7bfee45dcbb2c1311d7f6e284d943: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10359"/><div sID="gen18483" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10359"/>8. By the law a Hebrew, after having been a bond-servant for six years, on the seventh was to be let go free (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.22">Ex 21:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12">De 15:12</reference>).<div eID="gen18483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zedekiah made a covenant--</hi>with solemn ceremonial in the temple (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.15">Jr 34:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.19">18, 19</reference>).<div eID="gen18484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them--</hi>bond-servants (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.9">Jr 34:9</reference>). <div eID="gen18485" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4b362eaadc6b1c3fbda354256206452403e2ef5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10360"/><div sID="gen18486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10360"/><hi type="bold">9. none ... serve himself of a Jew--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.25.39-Lev.25.46">Le 25:39-46</reference>). <div eID="gen18486" type="x-p"/>
entries.c31b34b04c6fff39da1716d944957dbc7059621e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10361"/><div sID="gen18487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10361"/>11. During the interruption of the siege by Pharaoh-hophra (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.34.21">Jr 34:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.22">22</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5-Jer.37.10">Jr 37:5-10</reference>), the Jews reduced their servants to bondage again. <div eID="gen18487" type="x-p"/>
entries.261c51102bf23649520f413c4c135f730a758f86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10362"/><div sID="gen18488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10362"/>13. The last year of Zedekiah was the sabbatical year. How just the retribution, that they who, against God's law and their own covenant, enslaved their brethren, should be doomed to bondage themselves: and that the bond-servants should enjoy the sabbatical freedom at the hands of the foe (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">Jr 52:16</reference>) which their own countrymen denied them! <div eID="gen18488" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bf53156280f4745b2d97e247ca49a5586fb5aaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10363"/><div sID="gen18489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10363"/><hi type="bold">14. At the end of seven years--</hi>that is, not on the eighth year, but within the limit of the seventh year, not later than the end of the seventh year (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.2">Ex 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.10">23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12">De 15:12</reference>). So "at the end of three years" (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.28">De 14:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.10">2Ki 18:10</reference>), and "after three days, I will rise again" (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.63">Mt 27:63</reference>), that is, on the third day (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.27.64">Mt 27:64</reference>). <div eID="gen18489" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ecbf1868adc2d119475896aa66c0e2eaf6b4864: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10364"/><div sID="gen18490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10364"/><hi type="bold">15. in the house ... called by my name--</hi>the usual place of making such covenants (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.3">2Ki 23:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.31">1Ki 8:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.10.29">Ne 10:29</reference>). <div eID="gen18490" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce2ef7f6b19636c2b1304be55d285c2c1b87f43f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10365"/><div sID="gen18491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10365"/><hi type="bold">16. polluted my name--</hi>by violating your oath (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.7">Ex 20:7</reference>). <div eID="gen18491" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd64380d0445f296b53bd1322c6c5b8975717f1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10366"/><div sID="gen18492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10366"/><hi type="bold">17. not ... proclaiming liberty--</hi>Though the Jews had ostensibly emancipated their bond-servants, they virtually did not do so by revoking the liberty which they had granted. God looks not to outward appearances, but to the sincere intention.<div eID="gen18492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I proclaim a liberty--</hi>retribution answering to the offense (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.2">Mt 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.18.32">18:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Ga 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.13">Jas 2:13</reference>). The Jews who would not give liberty to their brethren shall themselves receive "a liberty" calamitous to them. God will manumit them from His happy and safe service (<reference osisRef="Ps.121.3">Psa 121:3</reference>), which is real "liberty" (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.45">Psa 119:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.36">Joh 8:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">2Co 3:17</reference>), only to pass under the terrible bondage of other taskmasters, the "sword," &c.<div eID="gen18493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be removed--</hi>The Hebrew expresses agitation (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.15.4">Jr 15:4</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.28.25">De 28:25</reference>, 48, 64, 65, as to the restless agitation of the Jews in their ceaseless removals from place to place in their dispersion. <div eID="gen18494" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd2091b2849f3aa5866b7e9797ac9085d00409d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10367"/><div sID="gen18495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10367"/><hi type="bold">18. passed between the parts thereof--</hi>The contracting parties in the "covenant" (not here the law in general, but their covenant made before God in His house to emancipate their slaves, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8">Jr 34:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.9">9</reference>) passed through the parts of the animal cut in two, implying that they prayed so to be cut in sunder (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.51">Mt 24:51</reference>; Greek, "cut in two") if they should break the covenant (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.10">Ge 15:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen18495" type="x-p"/>
entries.aad1acdadaa950b9c70d720c726422b19c997756: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10368"/><div sID="gen18496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10368"/><hi type="bold">20. I will even give--</hi>resuming the sentence begun, but not completed (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.18">Jr 34:18</reference>), "I will give," &c.<div eID="gen18496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek their life--</hi>implacably: satisfied with nothing short of their blood; not content with booty.<div eID="gen18497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dead bodies--</hi>The breakers of the covenant shall be cut in pieces, as the calf between whose parts they passed. <div eID="gen18498" type="x-p"/>
entries.b00e9df5ffa2b96f4cf5e5160d22dcd3a777a7e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10369"/><div sID="gen18499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10369"/><hi type="bold">21. gone up--</hi>that is, raised the siege in order to meet Pharaoh-hophra (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.7-Jer.37.10">Jr 37:7-10</reference>). The departure of the Chaldeans was a kind of manumission of the Jews; but as their manumission of their bond-servants was recalled, so God revoked His manumission of them from the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen18499" type="x-p"/>
entries.4790e6e69d4df696f0d69ba5827d2ea729d84d5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10370"/><div sID="gen18500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10370"/><hi type="bold">22. I will command--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar, impelled unconsciously by a divine instigation, returned on the withdrawal of the Egyptians. <chapter eID="Jer.34"/>

entries.40c2b6cf2071c95c66ea9adb21bd78a11db44b85: <div eID="gen30258" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30259" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30260" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30260" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30259" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30261" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains two prophecies: the first, delivered during the siege of Jerusalem, predicts to Zedekiah the taking and burning of the city, with his own peaceful death and honorable burial, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7">Jer 34:1-7</reference>. The second was delivered when the Chaldeans had for some time broken up the siege. It reproves the Jews for their conduct towards their brethren of the poorer sort, whom they released, by a solemn covenant, from bondage, in the extremity of their danger; but compelled to return to it when they thought that danger over, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.11">Jer 34:8-11</reference>. For this God threatens them with the sword, pestilence, and famine; and with the return of the Chaldeans, who should take the city, destroy it and the other cities by fire, and make an utter desolation of the whole land of Judea, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.12-Jer.34.22">Jer 34:12-22</reference>. <div eID="gen30261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30262" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30263" type="x-p"/> The word which came unto Jeremiah - This discourse was delivered in the tenth year of the reign of Zedekiah. The chapter contains two discourses; one, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7">Jer 34:1-7</reference>, which concerns the taking of the city, and Zedekiah's captivity and death; the other, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.22">Jer 34:8-22</reference>, which is an invective against the inhabitants of Jerusalem for having Hebrew male and female slaves. These, having been manumitted at the instance of the prophet, were afterwards brought back by their old masters, and put in the same thraldom; for which God threatens them with severe judgments. <div eID="gen30263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30264" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar - and all his army, and all the kingdoms of the earth of his dominion - That is, his army was composed of soldiers gathered out of Babylon, and out of all his tributary dominions: one hundred and twenty provinces.
entries.96f9f68812dd6453bd24f123128256494bda5be2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30265" type="x-p"/> He shall burn it with fire - This was a newly-added circumstance. Among many ancient nations they burned the bodies of the more illustrious dead. Odours were used in the burning: they then gathered the ashes, and put them into an urn or pitcher, sometimes into a strong vessel, and buried them. Many of these have been digged up in different parts of England, where the Romans had stations.
entries.12b552c4ea9658705bd26d3824fdc07499049b84: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30266" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not escape - This, however, he had attempted, but was taken in his flight. See <reference osisRef="Jer.39.4">Jer 39:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.52.7">Jer 52:7</reference>, etc.
entries.9331d6afad914c350ead459a06d33f96c5340fc3: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30267" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt die in peace - Thou shalt not die a violent death; and at thy death thou shalt have all those funereal solemnities which were usual at the demise of kings. See <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2Chr 16:14</reference>. <div eID="gen30267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30268" type="x-p"/> So shall they burn odours for thee - Scented wood and other odoriferous substances are placed on the funeral pile of the rich Hindoos, and burned with the body. <div eID="gen30268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30269" type="x-p"/> And they will lament thee, saying, Ah lord! - They will recite the funeral dirge that begins with those words. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jer.22.18">Jer 22:18</reference> (note).
entries.fa827a2649df6eba251265fb98f456e6e1c65314: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30270" type="x-p"/> Spake all these Words unto Zedekiah - He delivered this message at the hazard of his life. Jeremiah feared God, and had no other fear.
entries.7334804617e50f51da3120031c3cbc0739ee83a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30271" type="x-p"/> Against Lachish, and against Azekah - These were two cities of Judah of considerable importance: they had been strongly fortified by Rehoboam, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.9-2Chr.11.11">2Chr 11:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.9">2Chr 32:9</reference>.
entries.668ed7e694c3119b36d2784ae12c6f8a718e7f84: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen30271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30272" type="x-p"/> The word that came unto Jeremiah - Here the second discourse begins, which was delivered probably a short time, even a few days, after the former. <div eID="gen30272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30273" type="x-p"/> Zedekiah had made a covenant - We find no account elsewhere of this covenant: "Every man should let his man-servant and his maid-servant go free;" i.e., as we learn from <reference osisRef="Jer.34.14">Jer 34:14</reference>, on the sabbatical year; for the seventh year was the year of release. See <reference osisRef="Deu.15.12">Deu 15:12</reference>.
entries.15aa6e86b74d4037c09ac34e4b13b4c519581955: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30274" type="x-p"/> But afterward they turned - They had agreed to manumit them at the end of the seventh year; but when the seventh year was ended, they recalled their engagement, and detained their servants. This, I believe, is what is here meant.
entries.59ee88afeca9931a71edbee652ac7c1ee743bcb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30275" type="x-p"/> Ye - polluted my name - Had made the covenant in my name, calling me to witness it; now ye have dishonored my name, by breaking that covenant, and acting contrary to my law.
entries.20953f3ba41c721bc88994c4112c9e4d35918871: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30276" type="x-p"/> I proclaim a liberty for you - Ye proclaimed liberty to your slaves, and afterward resumed your authority over them; and I had in consequence restrained the sword from cutting you off: but now I give liberty to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine, and to the captivity, to destroy and consume you, and enslave you: for ye shall be removed to all the kingdoms of the earth. The prophet loves to express the conformity between the crime and its punishment. You promised to give liberty to your enslaved brethren; I was pleased, and bound the sword in its sheath. You broke your promise, and brought them again into bondage; I gave liberty to the sword, pestilence, and famine, to destroy multitudes of you, and captivity to take the rest. Thus you are punished according to your crimes, and in the punishment you may see the crime. Sword, pestilence, and famine are frequently joined together, as being often the effects of each other. The sword or war produces famine; famine, the pestilence.
entries.6e5badb2c55f0e31435cf55f6a02a4833fc35ede: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30277" type="x-p"/> When they cut the calf in twain, and passed between the parts thereof - This was the ancient and most solemn way of making a covenant. <div eID="gen30277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30278" type="x-p"/> 1. A calf as sacrifice was offered to God to secure his approbation and support. <div eID="gen30278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30279" type="x-p"/> 2. The victim was then exactly divided from the nose to the rump; the spinal marrow being divided longitudinally, in the most careful manner, that the half of it might remain on each side. <div eID="gen30279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30280" type="x-p"/> 3. These divided parts were laid opposite to each other, a passage being left between them. <div eID="gen30280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30281" type="x-p"/> 4. The contracting parties entered this passage at each end, met in the middle, and there took the covenant oath; adjudging themselves to death should they break this covenant. <div eID="gen30281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30282" type="x-p"/> 5. Then they both feasted on the victim. In reference to this last circumstance, God says he will give their bodies for meat to the fowls of heaven and to the beasts. This is a farther conformity between the crime and the punishment. See my notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9-Gen.15.17">Gen 15:9-17</reference> (note).
entries.ca89671f2cb78a63c14c6c95f21e648c568b657a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen30282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30283" type="x-p"/> The king of Babylon's army, which are gone up from you - Nebuchadnezzar, hearing that there was an Egyptian army coming to the relief of Jerusalem, raised the siege, went out, and met and defeated the Egyptians. It was in the interim this prophecy was delivered.
entries.d2c318b86dd64e5bab90db8427ff5f0eda07d0b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30284" type="x-p"/> I will - cause them to return - They did return; re-invested the city; and, after an obstinate defense, took it, plundered it, and burned it to the ground, taking Zedekiah and his princes captive.  <chapter eID="Jer.34"/> <div eID="gen30284" type="x-p"/>

entries.b1cc6d17b699cfa37b6e22996122dc4866a343d2: <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1">Jer 34:1</reference> <hi type="italic">The message to Zedekiah</hi> is regarded by Hitzig, Ewald, Graf, Nägelsbach, etc. as a supplement to Jer 32:1., and as giving, in its complete form, the prophecy to which Jer 32:3. was referred, as the reason of the confinement of Jeremiah in the court of the prison. Certainly it is so far true that Jeremiah, in <reference osisRef="Jer.34.2-Jer.34.5">Jer 34:2-5</reference>, expresses himself more fully regarding the fate of King Zedekiah at the fall of Jerusalem into the hands of the Chaldeans than in <reference osisRef="Jer.32.3-Jer.32.5">Jer 32:3-5</reference>; Jer 21:3., and <reference osisRef="Jer.37.17">Jer 37:17</reference>; but we are not warranted in drawing the inference that this message forms a historical appendix or supplement to Jer 32:3., and was the occasion or reason of Jeremiah’s imprisonment. See, on the contrary, the remarks on Jer 32:3. It is not given here as an appendix to explain the reason of the prophet’s imprisonment, but as a prophecy from which we may see how King Zedekiah was forewarned, from the very beginning of the siege, of what its issue would be, that he might frame his conduct accordingly. Nor does it belong to the period when Nebuchadnezzar, after beating off the Egyptians who had come to the relief of the beleaguered city, had returned to the siege of Jerusalem, but to the earliest period of the siege, when Zedekiah might still cherish the hope of defeating and driving off the Chaldeans through the help of the Egyptians. - According to <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1">Jer 34:1</reference>, the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah when "Nebuchadnezzar and," i.e., with, "all his host, and all the kingdoms of the land of the dominion of his hand, and all the nations, were fighting against Jerusalem and all her towns." The words are multiplied to represent the strength of the Chaldean army, so as to deepen the impression of overpowering might, against which resistance is vain. The army consists of men drawn from all the kingdoms of the territory he rules, and of all nations. ארץ ממשׁלת means the same as ארץ ממשׁלתּו, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.28">Jer 51:28</reference>, the territory over which his dominion, which includes many kingdoms, extends. The lxx have omitted "all the nations" as superfluous. See a like conglomeration of words in a similar description, Eze 26:7. "All her towns" are the towns of Judah which belong to Jerusalem; see Jer 19:15. According to <reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">Jer 34:7</reference>, the strong towns not yet taken are meant, especially those strongly fortified, <hi type="italic">Lachish</hi> and <hi type="italic">Azekah</hi> in the plain (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.39">Jos 15:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference>), the former of which is shown still under the name <hi type="italic">Um Lakhis</hi>, while the latter is to be sought for in the vicinity of <hi type="italic">Socho</hi>; see on <reference osisRef="Josh.10.3">Jos 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>, and 2Ch 11:9. - Jeremiah is to say to the king:
entries.562958edc81607dcb8ec676da52ce8eef1d7adff: <reference osisRef="Jer.34.2-Jer.34.7">Jer 34:2-7</reference> <hi type="italic">"Thus saith Jahveh: Behold, I will deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, that he may burn it with fire. </hi> Jer 34:3. <hi type="italic">And thou shalt not escape from his hand, but shalt certainly be seized and delivered into his hand; and thine eyes shall see the eyes of the king of Babylon, and his mouth shall speak with thy mouth, and thou shalt go to Babylon. </hi> Jer 34:4. <hi type="italic">But hear the word of Jahveh, O Zedekiah, king of Judah. Thus saith Jahveh concerning thee: Thou shalt not die by the sword. </hi> Jer 34:5. <hi type="italic">In peace shalt thou die; and as with the burnings of thy fathers, the former kings who were before thee, so shall they make a burning for thee, and they shall wail for thee, [crying,] 'Alas, lord!' for I have spoken the word, saith Jahveh. - </hi> On <reference osisRef="Jer.34.2">Jer 34:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.3">Jer 34:3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.32.3">Jer 32:3</reference>-5. "But hear," <reference osisRef="Jer.34.4">Jer 34:4</reference>, introduces an exception to what has been said before; but the meaning of <reference osisRef="Jer.34.4">Jer 34:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">Jer 34:5</reference> is disputed. They are usually understood in this say: Zedekiah shall be carried into exile to Babylon, but shall not be killed with the sword, or executed, but shall die a peaceful death, and be buried with royal honours. But C. B. Michaelis, Venema, Hitzig, and Graf take the words as an exception that will occur, should Zedekiah follow the advice given him to deliver himself up to the king of Babylon, instead of continuing the struggle. Then what is denounced in <reference osisRef="Jer.34.3">Jer 34:3</reference> will not happen; Zedekiah shall not be carried away to Babylon, but shall die as king in Jerusalem. This view rests on the hypothesis that the divine message has for its object to induce the king to submit and give up himself (cf. Jer 38:17.). But this supposition has no foundation; and what must be inserted, as the condition laid before Zedekiah, "if thou dost willingly submit to the king of Babylon," is quite arbitrary, and incompatible with the spirit of the word, "But hear the word of Jahveh," for in this case <reference osisRef="Jer.34.4">Jer 34:4</reference> at least would require to run, "Obey the word of Jahveh" (שׁמע בּדבר ), as Jer 38:20. To take the words שׁמע דברin the sense, "Give ear to the word, obey the word of Jahveh," is not merely inadmissible grammatically, but also against the context; for the word of Jahveh which Zedekiah is to hear, gives no directions as to how he is to act, but is simply an intimation as to what the end of his life shall be: to change or avert this does not stand in his power, so that we cannot here think of obedience or disobedience. The message in <reference osisRef="Jer.34.4">Jer 34:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">Jer 34:5</reference> states more in detail what that was which lay before Zedekiah: he shall fall into the hands of the king of Babylon, be carried into exile in Babylon, yet shall not die a violent death through the sword, but die peacefully, and be buried with honour - not, like Jehoiakim, fall in battle, and be left unmourned and unburied (Jer 22:18.). This intimation accords with the notices given elsewhere as to the end of Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jer 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.5-Jer.39.7">Jer 39:5-7</reference>). Although Zedekiah died a prisoner in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference>), yet his imprisonment would not necessarily be an obstacle in the way of an honourable burial after the fashion of his fathers. When Jehoiachin, after an imprisonment of thirty-seven years, was raised again to royal honours, then also might there be accorded not merely a tolerably comfortable imprisonment to Zedekiah himself, but to the Jews also, at his death, the permission to bury their king according to their national custom. Nor is anything to be found elsewhere contrary to this view of the words. The supposition that Zedekiah caused the prophet to be imprisoned on account of this message to him, which Nägelsbach has laboured hard to reconcile with the common acceptation of the passage, is wholly devoid of foundation in fact, and does not suit the time into which this message falls; for Jeremiah was not imprisoned till after the time when the Chaldeans were obliged for a season to raise the siege, on the approach of the Egyptians, and that, too, not at the command of the king, but by the watchman at the gate, on pretence that he was a deserter. "Thou shalt die in peace," in contrast with "thou shalt die by the sword," marks a peaceful death on a bed of sickness in contrast with execution, but not (what Graf introduces into the words) in addition, his being deposited in the sepulchre of his fathers. "With the burnings of thy fathers," etc., is to be understood, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2Ch 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.19">2Ch 21:19</reference>, of the burning of aromatic spices in honour of the dead; for the burning of corpses was not customary among the Hebrews: see on 2Ch 16:14. On "alas, lord!" see Jer 22:18. This promise is strengthened by the addition, "for I have spoken the word," where the emphasis lies on the אני: <hi type="italic">I</hi> the Lord have spoken the word, which therefore shall certainly be fulfilled. - In <reference osisRef="Jer.34.6">Jer 34:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">Jer 34:7</reference> it is further remarked in conclusion, that Jeremiah addressed these words to the king during the siege of Jerusalem, when all the cities of Judah except Lachish and Azekah were already in the power of the Chaldeans. ערי is not in apposition to ערי יהוּדה, but belongs to נשׁארוּ: "they were left among the towns of Judah as strong cities;" i.e., of the strong cities of Judah, they alone had not yet been conquered.
entries.42ae98c33981d02c4f193a598cc2e4eb29ff34eb: <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.11">Jer 34:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen14257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14258" type="x-p"/> Threatening because of the Re-enslavement of the Liberated Hebrew Men-and Maid-servants. - <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.11">Jer 34:8-11</reference> describe the occasion of the word of the Lord, which follows in <reference osisRef="Jer.34.12">Jer 34:12</reference>-22. It came to Jeremiah <hi type="italic">"after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem, to proclaim liberty to them, that every one should send away his man-servant, or his maid-servant, being a Hebrew or Hebrewess, so that none should impose servitude on any one of them who was a Jew, his brother. </hi> Jer 34:10. <hi type="italic">And all the princes and all the people who entered into the covenant obeyed, each one setting free his man-servant and his maid-servant, and not imposing servitude on them any more: they obeyed and each one set them free. </hi> Jer 34:11. <hi type="italic">But they turned round afterwards, and brought back the servants and the handmaids whom they had set free, and brought them under subjection, for servants and for handmaids."</hi> The covenant which Zedekiah concluded with all the people at Jerusalem, according to what follows, consisted in a solemn vow made before the Lord in the temple, probably confirmed by sacrifices, to set free the male and female slaves of Hebrew descent, in conformity with the law, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.1-Exod.21.4">Exo 21:1-4</reference>; Deu 15:12. <div eID="gen14258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14259" type="x-p"/> The law required the gratuitous manumission of these after seven years of service. This time, indeed, is not mentioned in our verses, but it is assumed as well known through the law. But, in the general departure of the people from the Lord and His commandments, the observance of this law had probably long been intermitted, so that, in consequence of the solemn engagement to obey it once more, a great number of Hebrew male and female slaves received their freedom, inasmuch as very many had served longer than seven years; however, we need not suppose that all bond men and women were liberated at once. The resolution, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.9">Jer 34:9</reference>, that every one should liberate his Hebrew man-or maid-servant, and that no one should continue to impose servitude on a Jew, his brother, i.e., compel him any longer to serve as a slave, is conditioned by the law, which is assumed as well known: this also accords with the expression לבלתּי עבד־בּם, which is used in a general way of the treatment of Hebrew men-and maid-servants, Lev 25:39. However, it is also possible that a liberation of all bond men and women took place without regard to the duration of their servitude, partly for the purpose of averting, by such obedience to the law, the calamity now threatening the city, and partly also to employ the liberated slaves in the defence of the city; for, according to Jer 34:21., the emancipation took place during the siege of Jerusalem, and after the departure of the Chaldeans the solemn promise was revoked. The expression קתא דרור, "to proclaim liberty," is taken from <reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Lev 25:10</reference>, but it does not prove that the manumission took place on a sabbath-or jubilee-year. להם refers <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi> to those who were bondmen and had a right to be set free. The general expression is explained by שׁלּח חפשׁים, and this again is more closely defined by לבלתּי עבד־בּם (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference>). אישׁ  בּיהוּדי אחיהוּ, (that no one should labour) "though a Jew, who is his brother," i.e., a fellow-countryman; i.e., that no one should impose servitude on a Jew, as being a compatriot. "To enter into a covenant" is to assume its obligation; cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.12">2Ch 15:12</reference>; Eze 16:8. The <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi> יכבישׁום receives, in the <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi>, the vowels of the Kal, since the Hiphil of this verb does not occur elsewhere, only the Kal, cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.10">2Ch 28:10</reference>; but the alteration is unnecessary - the Hiphil may intensify the active meaning.
entries.5b82b2ddfea5d9b619ceb694fa1e8018116dadae: <reference osisRef="Jer.34.12">Jer 34:12</reference> <hi type="italic">The threat of punishment. - </hi> Jer 34:12. <hi type="italic">"Then came the word of Jahveh to Jeremiah from Jahveh, saying: </hi> Jer 34:13. <hi type="italic">Thus saith Jahveh, the God of Israel, 'I made a covenant with your fathers in the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from a house of bondmen, saying, </hi> Jer 34:14. <hi type="italic">At the end of seven years shall ye set free each man his brother, who is a Hebrew that sold himself to thee; and he shall serve thee six years, then shalt thou send him away from thee free: but your fathers hearkened not unto me, nor inclined their ear. </hi> Jer 34:15. <hi type="italic">But you had turned just now, and had done what is right in mine eyes, because each man proclaimed liberty to his neighbour, ad ye had made a covenant before me in the house on which my name is called. </hi> Jer 34:16. <hi type="italic">But ye turned again and profaned my name, and each one made his man-servant and his handmaid, whom he had sent away free, at their pleasure, to return, and ye brought them into subjection, to be men-and maid-servants to you. </hi> Jer 34:17. <hi type="italic">Therefore, thus saith Jahveh, Ye have not hearkened unto me in proclaiming liberty each man to his brother, and each man to his neighbour: behold, I proclaim a liberty for you, saith Jahveh, to the sword, to the pestilence, and to famine, and I will deliver you up for maltreatment to all the kingdoms of the earth. </hi> Jer 34:18. <hi type="italic">And I shall make the men who have transgressed my covenant, that have not kept the words of the covenant which they concluded before me, like the calf which they cut in two, and between whose pieces they passed. </hi> Jer 34:19. <hi type="italic">The princes of Judah and the princes of Jerusalem, the courtiers, and the priests, and all he people of the land, who passed through between the pieces of the calf, </hi> Jer 34:20. <hi type="italic">Them will I give into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their life, so that their corpses shall be for food to the birds of heaven and to the beasts of the earth. </hi> Jer 34:21. <hi type="italic">And Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his princes will I give into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their life, and into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon, that has departed from against you. </hi> Jer 34:22. <hi type="italic">Behold, I will command, saith Jahveh, and will make them return to this city, and they shall fight against it, and shall take it, and shall burn it with fire; and the cities of Judah will I make a desolation, without an inhabitant."</hi>
entries.7bbeecf84ac843e4911f9c3b26667ebd87b8ee97: <reference osisRef="Jer.34.13-Jer.34.16">Jer 34:13-16</reference> <div eID="gen14259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14260" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Jer.34.13-Jer.34.16">Jer 34:13-16</reference> the Lord sets before the people and their rulers their new offence; in <reference osisRef="Jer.34.17-Jer.34.22">Jer 34:17-22</reference> He announces to them the punishment for this new deed by which the covenant is broken. In order to place the transgression in its proper light, He mentions, first of all, that, when He led Israel out of Egypt, He concluded with them a covenant to the effect that every one of them should set free his Hebrew servant at the end of seven years; He also mentions that their fathers had transgressed this covenant (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.13">Jer 34:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.14">Jer 34:14</reference>). The designation of Egypt as a house of bondmen, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.13.3">Exo 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.14">Exo 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.20.2">Exo 20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.12">Deu 6:12</reference>, etc., possesses a special emphasis, and points to what is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.15.15">Deu 15:15</reference> as the motive for obeying the law referred to in the address. Because Israel was a servant in Egypt, and the Lord has redeemed him out of this house of bondmen, therefore must they not treat as slaves their brethren who had fallen into poverty, but set them free after six years of service. The expression "at the end (after the lapse) of seven years" is to be understood in the same way as the expression "after eight days." As this just means "when seven days are completed," so also, according to the law, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.2">Exo 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12">Deu 15:12</reference>, the emancipation was to follow in the seventh year, after six full years of service. "Who sold himself to thee" is an expression copied from Deu 15:12. - From this sin of their fathers they had now for a little turned away, and, in a solemn covenant, resolved to free the bondmen, as the law decreed (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.15">Jer 34:15</reference>); but they have immediately profaned the name of the Lord again by revoking this decree, viz., by breaking the covenant made before God. לנפשׁם, "according to their pleasure," like eלנפשׁהּ, Deu 21:14.
entries.b8fb94730cc896a364ccb52f06712dd2f4fd2870: <reference osisRef="Jer.34.17-Jer.34.18">Jer 34:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen14260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14261" type="x-p"/> The announcement of punishment. Because ye have not hearkened, by proclaiming, every one, liberty to his bondman (this certainly had been done, but was again undone by annulling the decree), therefore I proclaim liberty for you; i.e., you, who have hitherto been my servants (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.55">Lev 25:55</reference>), I discharge from this relation, - deliver you up to your fate as regards the sword, etc., that the sword, famine, and pestilence may have power over you. For לזועה see Jer 15:4. - In <reference osisRef="Jer.34.18">Jer 34:18</reference> the construction is disputed. Many, including Luther, take העגל as the second object to נתתּי: "I will make the men...the calf," i.e., like the calf. But, though נתן is frequently construed with a double accusative with the meaning of making some thing another thing (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.34.22">Jer 34:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.5">Gen 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.7.1">Exo 7:1</reference>), yet in such a case the predicative-object does not readily take the article. Moreover, נתן, in the sense required here, to make like = treat as, is joined with כּ, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa 41:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.6">Eze 28:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.42.30">Gen 42:30</reference>; 1Ki 10:27, etc. Finally, Rosenmüller objects: <hi type="italic">continuata versu</hi> 19 <hi type="italic">personarum descriptio et repetitio verbi</hi> yṭitanfw̱ <reference osisRef="Jer.34.20">Jer 34:20</reference> <hi type="italic">vix permittunt, propositionem hoc versu absolvi</hi>. For these reasons, L. de Dieu, Rosenmüller, Ewald, and Graf have taken העגל as being in apposition to הבּרית, and the enumeration "princes of Judah," etc., <reference osisRef="Jer.34.19">Jer 34:19</reference>, as a continuation or exposition of האנשׁים, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.18">Jer 34:18</reference>, and ונתתּי אותם, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.20">Jer 34:20</reference>, as a resumption of the same words in Jer 34:18. According to this view, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.18-Jer.34.20">Jer 34:18-20</reference> would form a series of appositions: "I will give the men...that have not kept the words of the covenant which they concluded before me...the princes of Judah who passed between the parts of the calf, - these will I give into the hands of their enemies." But, apart from the consideration that the enumeration of the covenant-breakers (viz., the princes of Judah, etc.), which is added by way of apposition in <reference osisRef="Jer.34.19">Jer 34:19</reference>, ought not to come in till after the apposition to הבּרית, which would be a harsh and complicated arrangement of the members of the sentence, this construction seems untenable for the following reasons: (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) "The calf that they cut," etc., which forms the explanatory apposition to "the covenant," is separated from it by the intervening clause, "which they made before me." And (<hi type="italic">b</hi>), even though we might modify this harshness by repeating את־דּברי before העגל, yet the mode of expression, "they have not performed the words of the calf which they cut in two, and between whose parts they passed," would be a very stiff and unnatural one for "they have not performed what they vowed or sware in presence of the parts of the calf which they had halved, and when they passed through between these pieces." With Maurer and Hitzig, therefore, we abide by the older view, which takes העגל as the second object to ונתתּי: "I will make the men...the calf," or, better, "like the calf which they cut in two," etc. The article is used with עגל because this predicate is more exactly determined by relative clauses, and העגל stands for כּעגל, since, as often happens, the כּ of likeness is dropped to give more point to the idea. We make <reference osisRef="Jer.34.19">Jer 34:19</reference> begin a new sentence, and take the names of this verse as objects absolute, which, by אותם following ונתתּי, are subordinated to the verb: "As for the princes of Judah...them shall I give...." - From <reference osisRef="Jer.34.18">Jer 34:18</reference> we see that, when alliances were entered into, the contracting parties slaughtered an עגל, "calf," i.e., a young bullock, cut it in two halves, and went through between the pieces that were placed opposite one another. See on <reference osisRef="Gen.15.10">Gen 15:10</reference> for details regarding this most ancient custom and its meaning: according to the account of Ephraem Syrus, it is of Chaldean origin. Thus are explained the phrases used to signify the making of a covenant. כּרת בּרית, <hi type="italic">to cut a covenant</hi>, ὅρκια τέμνειν, <hi type="italic">faedus ferire</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">ferienda hostia faedus facere</hi>. We cannot with certainty infer, from the threatening pronounced in this passage, that this rite originally signified nothing more than that he who broke his promise would be treated like the animal that had been slaughtered. For the threatening is merely a conclusion drawn from the sacred act; but this does not exclude a deeper meaning of the rite. <div eID="gen14261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14262" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.34.19-Jer.34.22">Jer 34:19-22</reference> give the real explanation of the threatening attached to the ritual of the covenant. Princes, officers of the court, priests and people, who have transgressed the covenant, shall die by the hand of the enemy, and perish ignominiously. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.34.20">Jer 34:20</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.7.33">Jer 7:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.4">Jer 16:4</reference>, etc. On סריסים see on Gen 37:36. King Zedekiah also, with his princes, his retinue, shall fall into the hand of his enemies, ay, into the hands of the Chaldeans, who have now withdrawn from Jerusalem (on עלה  see on <reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jer 21:2</reference>). See also <reference osisRef="Gen.37.5">Gen 37:5</reference>-8. The Example of the Rechabites <div eID="gen14262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14263" type="x-p"/> By the command of God, Jeremiah brings the family of the Rechabites (who had fled for refuge to Jerusalem before the approach of the Chaldeans) into one of the chambers of the temple, and sets before them some wine to drink (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.1-Jer.35.5">Jer 35:1-5</reference>). They decline to drink, because the head of their family had forbidden them the use of wine, as well as the possession of houses and the cultivation of the soil, and had commanded them to live in tents (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.6-Jer.35.11">Jer 35:6-11</reference>). Jeremiah is to put this before the people of Judah. The Rechabites faithfully observe the command of their ancestor, while the people of Judah transgress the commands of their God, which are continually presented to them (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.12-Jer.35.16">Jer 35:12-16</reference>). Therefore the threatened calamity shall fall upon Judah; but the house of Rechab, as a reward for their faithfulness to the injunctions of their ancestor, shall continue for ever (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.17-Jer.35.19">Jer 35:17-19</reference>). <div eID="gen14263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14264" type="x-p"/> According to <reference osisRef="Jer.35.1">Jer 35:1</reference>, this word of the Lord came to Jeremiah in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim, and, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.35.11">Jer 35:11</reference>, previous to the arrival of Nebuchadnezzar and his host before Jerusalem; therefore perhaps in the summer of the year 606 b.c., for Jerusalem was taken for the first time by Nebuchadnezzar in the ninth month (December) of that year.  <chapter eID="Jer.34"/> <div eID="gen14264" type="x-p"/>

entries.933176ae52a93c9a0d757ddbd176fca8b0b6d46e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.34.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.34.1" sID="gen62553" type="section"/> <div sID="gen62554" type="x-p"/>It is no wonder, nor ought it to be deemed useless, that the Prophet so often repeats the same things, for we know how great was the hardness of the people with whom he had to do. Here, then, he tells us that he was sent to King Zedekiah when the city was besieged by Nebuchadnezzar and his whole army. The Prophet mentions the circumstances, by which we may understand how formidable that siege was, for Nebuchadnezzar had not brought a small force, but had armed many and various people. Hence the Prophet here expressly mentions <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of the earth and the nations who were, under his dominion</hi><div eID="gen62554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen62555" type="x-p"/>Zedekiah was then the king at Jerusalem, and there remained two other cities safe, as we shall hereafter see; but it is evident how unequal he must have been to contend with an army so large and powerful. Nebuchadnezzar was a monarch; the kingdom of Israel had been cut off, which far exceeded in number the kingdom of Judah; and he had subdued all the neighboring nations. Such a siege then ought to have immediately taken away from the Jews every hope of deliverance; and yet the Prophet shews that the king was as yet resolute, and there was still a greater obstinacy among the people. But Zedekiah was not overbearing; we find that he was not so proud and so cruel as tyrants are wont to be: as then he was not of a ferocious disposition, we hence see how great must have been the pride of the whole people, and also their perverseness against God, when they made the king to be so angry with the Prophet. Yet the state of things as described ought to have subdued his passion; for as ungodly men are elevated by prosperity, so they ought to be humbled when oppressed with adversity. The king himself, as well as the people, were reduced to the greatest extremities, and yet they would not be admonished by God’s Prophet; and hence it is expressly said in <reference osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.16">2 Chronicles 36:16</reference>, that Zedekiah did not regard the word of the Prophet, though he spoke from the mouth of the Lord, by whom he had been sent.<div eID="gen62555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen62556" type="x-p"/>The sum of this prophecy is as follows: — He first says that the <hi type="italic">word was given him by Jehovah; </hi>and secondly, he points out the time, for what reason we have already stated. For if he had reproved Zedekiah when there was peace and quietness, and when there was no fear of danger, the king might have been easily excited, as it is usual, against the Prophet. But when he saw the city surrounded on every side by so large and powerful an army, — when he saw collected so many from the kingdoms of the earth, — so many nations, that he could hardly muster up the thousandth part of the force of his enemies,wthat he could not and would not, notwithstanding all this, submit to God and acknowledge his vengeance just, — this was an instance of extreme blindness, and a proof that he was become as it were estranged in mind. But God had thus blinded him, because his purpose was, as it is said elsewhere, to bring an extreme punishment on the people. The blindness, then, and the madness of the king, was an evidence of God’s wrath towards the whole people; for Zedekiah might have appeased God if he had repented. It was then God’s will that he should have been of an intractable disposition, in order that he might by such perverseness and obstinacy bring on himself utter ruin.<div eID="gen62556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen62557" type="x-p"/>He mentions <hi type="italic">Nebuchadnezzar </hi>and <hi type="italic">his whole army; </hi>he afterwards describes the army more particularly, <hi type="italic">with all the kingdoms under his dominion, and all nations</hi> When Jerusalem was in this condition, the Prophet was sent to the king. The substance of the message follows, even that the city was doomed to destruction, because God had resolved to deliver it into the hand of the enemy. This was a very sad message to Zedekiah. Hypocrites, we know, seek flatteries in their calamities; while God spares them they will not bear to be reproved, and they reject wise counsels, and even become exasperated when God’s Prophets exhort them to repent. But when God begins to smite them, they wish all to partake of their misfortunes; and then also they accuse God’s servants of cruelty, as though they insulted their misery by setting their sins before them.<div eID="gen62557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen62558" type="x-p"/>This is what we are taught by daily experience. When any one of the common people, at the time when God does not chasten them either by disease or poverty, or any other adversity, is admonished, the petulant answer is, “What do you mean? in what respect am I worthy of blame? I am conscious of no evil.” Thus hypocrites boast as long as God bears with them, and though his kindness spares them. But when any adversity happens to them, when any one is laid on his bed, when another is bereaved of a son or a wife, or in any way visited with afltietion, — if then God’s judgment is set before them, they think that a grievous wrong is done to them: “What! have I not evils enough without any addition? I expected comfort from God’s servants, but they exaggerate my calamities.” In short, hypocrites are never in a fit condition to receive God’s reproofs.<div eID="gen62558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen62559" type="x-p"/>There is then no doubt but that Jeremiah knew that his message would be intolerable to King Zedekiah, and to his people. However, he boldly declared, as we shall see, what God had committed to him.
